attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Firm 'will' with the antecedent 'once they do make stuff up' kept, and no deadline. This is a firm forecast, so it can be scored.

contract.note: The plain reading that one documented LLM-to-LLM transfer counts is ordinary and fair. Excluding conventional snippets is a fair limit. Reading 'stuff up like that' broadly is reasonable but is the evaluator's choice, and it decides the result.

evidence.note: Ars traces the false egg answer to Quora's GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) output and shows it in a Google Featured Snippet. That establishes the LLM fabrication. A conventional snippet is not a generative receiver, so this item does not show the outcome.

Futurism, dated Sept 2023. Per its located SGE paragraphs, the reporter got the same false answer from Google's generative SGE, which traces it to the Quora LLM output. The excerpt shown mainly covers the snippet. Later correction does not undo the occurrence.

reviews.rationale: Antecedent met: LLMs fabricated content (e1). The early-resolution rule is met by a dated September 2023 case: false GPT-3 output on Quora reappeared in Google's generative SGE (e2). This shows the phenomenon happened, not that it is widespread. The visible excerpt mostly describes the snippet, so the SGE transfer rests on e2's located paragraphs.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. The embedded examples are images he selected.

semantics.note: Faithfully keeps 'infested', Amazon, and people using GPT to make low-quality books.

contract.note: The plain reading (a recurring presence of defective GPT-made books, not most books) is fair. Requiring GPT provenance follows his own words, though reading GPT strictly is somewhat demanding.

evidence.note: Shows dozens of incoherent books on Amazon in June 2023, but does not establish GPT or even AI provenance.
Fake books credited to Friedman on Amazon. Her ChatGPT attribution is her own inference ('most likely'), not verified provenance.
Confirms the books were incoherent but offers poor translation as another explanation, which weakens a GPT attribution.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows defective books on Amazon during the period, but none has established GPT provenance. Friedman's is an inference, and Daily Dot suggests bad translation. Nothing shows the books were not GPT-made either. The contract requires availability, defects and GPT provenance for the same books, and the packet does not settle that.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'It's on' is fairly rendered as 'already under way'. The claim states a current condition.

contract.note: The plain reading (LLM junk already degrading parts of the internet, without an internet-wide decline) is ordinary and fair. The Feb–Aug 2023 window comes from his own retrospective.

evidence.note: NewsGuard, May 2023: 49 sites that appear AI-generated, some pushing false narratives such as a fake Biden death report, identified by chatbot artifacts. It notes most sites were not misinformation and some operators denied using AI.
NewsGuard, May 19, 2023: 125 sites with unedited chatbot error messages, poorly written clickbait, and false claims. This is a count of sites found, not a measure of growth.

reviews.rationale: Two dated NewsGuard investigations within the period document a growing set of public sites with LLM artifacts, quality defects and false claims. That meets the support condition. Most sites not spreading misinformation does not defeat the claim, because quality defects also count. Neither report measures the internet as a whole.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. The recipe is an embedded example he chose.

semantics.note: Keeps his words 'fully capable' and 'disconcerting recipe from last week'. It is a capability claim.

contract.note: The plain capability reading (an LLM can produce seriously harmful advice) is ordinary. Counting adversarial inputs as proof of capability is fair. Identifying the embedded recipe as the Savey bot's is an inference.

evidence.note: Ars: the GPT-3.5-based Savey Meal-bot gave a bleach-and-ammonia recipe on Aug 4, 2023, inside the target period. It explains the chloramine danger and that a later reproduction was blocked.
Guardian, Aug 10: the bot presented the toxic mix as a refreshing drink, and the operator responded. The chemistry label should read chloramines rather than chlorine gas.
ChatGPT refused the same inputs. This limits generalising across deployments but does not undercut the capability shown.

reviews.rationale: A GPT-3.5 application produced dangerous advice on Aug 4, 2023, recommending a toxic chemical mix as a drink. The case was reported Aug 10, about a week before the post. ChatGPT refusing the same inputs shows not every LLM does this, but the claim is only about capability, so it is supported.
